Clock 3: 624(d)(4) notice is due before the delay takes effect (or as soon as practicable); SASC sec. 501 would require notice to Congress within 30 days of a delay (CRS).
Clock 6: 624(d)(5) six months unless the Secretary concerned specifies a further period.
Clock 12: conditional reasoning ('Without written grounds ... there is little on paper ...'); follows from the statute and reporting. Untagged; see flags.

Clock 18, on a dial labeled 'Months since the board selected the officer': '...the law removes the name from the list.' 629(c)(4): the eligibility period runs from the date the President approves the list to 'the first day of the eighteenth month following the month' of approval, not from board selection; 629(c)(2): the President (delegated to SecDef, EO 13598) 'may extend that period ... by an additional 12 months'; 629(c)(3) exception for information held by another agency. Retirement: relays say 'typically' (Clash) / 'most' (Independent).
verdicts.fix: Eighteen months after the President approves the list: if the officer has not been appointed and the Senate has not consented, the law removes the name, unless the period has been extended by up to 12 months. flags: MS NOW's Nov. 9 article (ms.now) could not be loaded: WebFetch client_error twice; archive.org not on the allowlist; shell egress blocked. Every MS NOW claim was checked against seven reports of it (Military.com, Raw Story, Daily Beast, Atlanta Black Star, Clash Report, The Independent and Mediaite via Yahoo). Relays differ on details (sources: 'a senior official' plus two officers vs 'three military officials'; officers affected: 'at least 12' vs 'more than a dozen'). An editor should read the MS NOW original before publishing, especially for c026, x018 and x021 to x024.

Statute the page misses: 10 U.S.C. 618(g) (since 1991) says that if a removal recommendation is accompanied by information not presented to the selection board, 'that information shall be made available to that officer' with 'a reasonable opportunity to submit comments.' This is the provision most on point for search printouts used to remove names, and it is stronger for the page's argument than 624(d), which covers delays only.

Lede and section framing: 'The law says the officer should be told why, in writing, and get to answer' is true for a delay under 624(d)(4) and for removal recommendations under 618(g), but not for a removal by the President under 629(a) generally. Most NYT cases are removals. The lede should say which.

Clock intro paragraph (untagged) says the law removes a name 'unless the Senate has already consented'; it omits the 12-month extension in 629(c)(2) and that the 18 months run from the President's approval of the list.
'40+' / '40-plus' (c001, c038, stat 1): the NYT says 'at least 40'. 'At least 40' is exact and avoids reading as 'more than 40'.

Vaccine data-then (x019): the order formally ended Jan. 10, 2023, when Austin rescinded it as the FY2023 NDAA required. 'until Congress required its end in the defense bill signed in December 2022; it was rescinded Jan. 10, 2023' is more exact.

Absence findings tagged WATCH (c005, c021, c027) are searches by Infera; Editorial Standard v2 section 2 treats 'we found no ...' as INFERENCE (search result). Passed as WATCH because each is an open item, but the label should be consistent site-wide.
Clock reading at 12 months (x016) is Infera's reasoning shown without a tag; consider INFERENCE.

Scope drift since June: search results show Hegseth removed six Army officers from a two-star list in Sept. 2026 (The Hill, foreignpolicyjournal; The Hill page failed to load). The 'by mid-June' scope keeps the 40+ figure accurate, but per Standard section 10 this is a review trigger for the lists table.
Other side: present and real (section 07: Parnell's statements, statutory authority, civilian-control argument). The RedState item (c034) needs its attribution fixed.
